title: Given an array that may contain duplicate integers, return all unique permutations.
shortTitle: Permutations II (with duplicates): sort then skip same-level duplicates
keyPoints: Sort the array so equal values are adjacent, then run permutation backtracking with a used[] array.
Skip nums[i] if it equals nums[i-1] and the previous equal element is not used (!used[i-1]), enforcing canonical left-to-right order.
The !used[i-1] condition ensures among equal values, an earlier copy is always placed before a later copy.
Flipping the condition to used[i-1] would keep duplicates and drop valid permutations.
Worst-case time is O(n * n!) for all-distinct elements, reduced when duplicates prune branches.
The same canonical-order trick is the general recipe for de-duplicating any permutation enumeration.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sort, then skip a duplicate value whose equal predecessor is unused at this branch to avoid repeated permutations.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Permutations II** – generate all unique orderings of an array that may contain duplicates.
- **Sort first** – places equal values adjacent for neighbor comparison.
- **used[] array** – tracks which elements are currently placed in the permutation path.
- **Skip guard** – skip `nums[i]` if `nums[i] == nums[i-1]` and `!used[i-1]`, enforcing canonical left-to-right placement of identical values.
- **Time** – O(n * n!) worst case for all-distinct elements.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India schedules processing batches where some are interchangeable (same type). Swapping two identical batches does not create a genuinely different schedule. By insisting identical batches are always placed in their fixed left-to-right order, you count each truly distinct schedule once.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Input: [1, 1, 2] (sorted)
  used = [F, F, F]

  Level 0:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ i=0: nums[0]=1, not used --> CHOOSE  │
  │   used=[T,F,F], path=[1]             │
  │                                      │
  │ i=1: nums[1]=1, nums[1]==nums[0]     │
  │   !used[0]? NO (used[0]=T)           │
  │   --> NOT skipped (previous is used)  │
  │   BUT wait: used[0]=T, so !used[0]=F │
  │   Skip condition FALSE --> CHOOSE     │
  │   Actually skip fires when !used=T    │
  │                                      │
  │ i=1 at level 0 (fresh):              │
  │   used=[F,F,F], !used[0]=T           │
  │   --> SKIP (would place 1b before 1a)│
  │                                      │
  │ i=2: nums[2]=2 --> CHOOSE            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Unique Permutations:
  [1, 1, 2]  [1, 2, 1]  [2, 1, 1]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Permutations II generates every unique ordering when the input contains duplicate values. I sort first so equal values are adjacent, then run the standard permutation backtracking with the used array, and I add one guard: I skip the current element if it equals the previous element and that previous equal element is not currently used in this branch. That guard fixes a canonical left-to-right order within each group of identical values, which is what removes the mirror-image duplicates.

The direction of the condition matters: testing `!used[i-1]` forces earlier copies to be placed before later copies. If I flipped it to `used[i-1]`, I would keep duplicates and drop valid permutations. The worst-case cost is O(n * n!) for all-distinct elements, reduced in practice as duplicates prune branches.

The same canonical-order trick is the general recipe for de-duplicating any permutation enumeration. It is the permutation analogue of the skip-same-level-duplicate pattern I use in Subsets II and Combination Sum II.

In my project at National Bank of India, a planner built processing schedules from job slots where several jobs were of identical type, and it needed every genuinely distinct schedule rather than reshuffles of interchangeable jobs. This sorted canonical-order technique produced each distinct schedule exactly once.

Remember one sentence: sort the array, skip any element whose equal predecessor is not used in the current branch, and each group of identical values is placed in canonical left-to-right order, generating each unique permutation exactly once.
